\chapter*{Reading guide}
This book explains how the two packages of the companion repository, \fea{} and \rom{}, are built, and checks that they do what is claimed for them. It is meant to be read with the repository open. This guide says how the two fit together, how a chapter is laid out, and what the marks in the text mean.

\section*{Working with the repository}

The book is tied to one pinned release of the repository, tag \booktag{}: every listing, number and code anchor refers to that release. Check out the tag before you run anything, or the output you see may differ from the output printed here. The two packages depend only on NumPy and SciPy. Either install them from the repository (each has its own \texttt{pyproject.toml}) or put the two \texttt{src} directories on the Python path. PyTorch is optional and is needed only for the parts that say so; PyVista is used for the three-dimensional figures of Chapter~\ref{ch:mesh}. The listings that print output assume the working directory named in their caption, and nothing else. The package tests are run with \texttt{pytest} from the repository root, and Appendix~\ref{ch:map} lists, chapter by chapter, which test files cover the topic.

\section*{How a chapter is laid out}

A chapter opens with a box that says what it is about and what you should be able to do afterwards, and then with a concrete problem. The technical sections follow the same order throughout: the problem, the mathematical structure, the implementation in the packages, then a \emph{Verification} section, a box of limits, a summary and exercises. Because the layout is the same in the full-order and the reduced-order chapters, a reader who has met one chapter knows where to look in the next. Chapter~\ref{ch:contact} was written first, and the other chapters follow its layout.

Algorithms are given as pseudocode, and a short paragraph after each says what it costs, how it fails and where the code is. Listings headed \emph{Try it} are complete, and the output printed under them is what the code produced; where the naive version is shown first, it is meant to be run too. Definitions and detours sit in blue sidenote boxes and can be skipped on a first reading. Code is cited as \anchor{importable.name}, and the code-map table near the end of each technical chapter says which names the chapter's own checks call: yes for every name, part for some, no for none. Code that is only reached through another routine counts as no, so that column is a lower bound on what the book exercises.

\section*{What the limits boxes and exercises are for}

The box on limits at the end of each chapter lists what was not tested, so that a result is not read as covering more than it does. It is worth reading before you rely on a method. The exercises are of three kinds, marked in the text: derivations, implementations (most extend a listing, and some ask you to reproduce a number of the book with different settings), and interpretations of a result. Where an exercise has a package test file behind it, the file is named.

\section*{Where the numbers come from}

Numbers in the text are generated by scripts that live with the book sources and enter the book as macros, so the number in the text is the one that was measured. The exception is the nine reproduction studies of Chapter~\ref{ch:verif}: their numbers are quoted from the author's reports and were not regenerated at the tag, and the text says so each time. Read the next section before you rely on any number in a Verification section.

\section*{Reading paths}

You can read straight through, but the book does not have to be read that way. A reader who comes for the reduction methods can start at Chapter~\ref{ch:pod} and go back to Chapters~\ref{ch:nonlin} and~\ref{ch:contact} when Chapters~\ref{ch:nonint} and~\ref{ch:hyper} need them. A reader who wants to extend the finite element package needs Parts~I and~II and can stop there. A reader who is deciding how far to trust the results should read the next section and Chapter~\ref{ch:verif}, which says what kind of evidence each number is.

\chapter*{How to read the verification sections}
Each chapter closes its technical part with a \emph{Verification} section, and three words are used there in a fixed sense. A \emph{unit test} is an automatic check in the package's test suite. \emph{Verification} asks whether the code solves the stated equations correctly, judged against an exact solution, an independent computation or an observed rate of convergence. \emph{Validation} asks whether the equations describe reality, judged against experiments. Nothing in this book is validation. A small error against a reference shows that the code does what the equations say; it does not show that the equations suit a particular structure, or that the code is right for cases nobody ran.

When you read a number in a Verification section, look next to it for the model and its loading, the solver settings, the reference value, the definition of the error, and the release and machine. The numbers in this draft come from a sandbox with two processors and are single runs. Timings move by tens of per cent between runs at these small sizes, so read them as orders of magnitude and not as benchmarks; they will be regenerated from the scripts of Appendix~\ref{ch:map} on the release machine before publication.

Reduced-order models come with a few extra conventions, set out in Appendix~\ref{ch:conv}. A speed-up refers to the online solve unless the text says otherwise, offline and online costs are given separately, errors are measured on parameters that were not used for training, and the benchmark models are small, so a speed-up at this size does not predict one at production size. When a method or a piece of code is listed but not run in this book, the last column of the chapter's code-map table says so, and the chapter's Limits box lists what was not tested. The notation follows the abbreviations, and Appendix~\ref{ch:gloss} is a glossary.
